cover.notes:
Hi, I'm Dylan Couzon. I do research in Developer Relations at Qdrant. Thanks for joining us here and on Zoom.

Say someone offers you a cheaper embedding model on Monday. What would it cost to try it? If you change both encoders, that's another pass over the corpus and another index. I wanted to try the cheaper half on its own.

[Trace the three paths into the cluster.] Each route makes a query vector and searches the same documents. One route makes its vector from a lookup table. I'll show you how I built it, then race it against the model that built the index.

cost.notes:
[Point to the score, then the two terms in the cost equation.] The score is a dot product between two unit vectors. I can take my time building the document vector because I get to reuse it. Every uncached query needs a fresh vector and a search. If an agent calls search several times, I pay that query cost several times.

For scale, I encoded the 2.7 million Wikipedia passages we'll search later on one RTX 3080. At a steady 141 passages per second, that's an estimated 5.3 GPU-hours of encoding. The run took 6.5 hours elapsed with a memory spill and a crash. Mine was a desktop, and it had opinions.

On the query side, Stella saw a median of 31 tokens including its instruction prompt. That's about 25 billion floating-point operations and 32 milliseconds on a laptop CPU with four threads. The mean gives about 10.3 elapsed hours for a million sequential queries, before search.

A swap of both encoders brings the passage job back and can leave you running two indexes during migration. What happens if I change just the function that makes the query vector?

flops.notes:
[Trace the three bars on the log scale.] A token takes a very different trip through each encoder. Stella sends it through 24 layers at width 1,024. Nano sends it through 12 layers at width 384. Zero uses its token ID to fetch a row, then pools and normalizes the rows.

For the transformer estimate I count the weights used in matrix multiplies, multiply by twice the token count, and add attention. That counts Stella's gated feed-forward block and Nano's projection on every token. At the median lengths, 31 tokens for Stella and 12 for Nano, I get 25.1 and 0.54 billion operations. Zero takes about 28,000. That's roughly 900,000 times less arithmetic than Stella and 19,000 times less than Nano.

Zero takes its name from the number of neural network passes it runs to encode a query. The lookup does arithmetic, and I still have an index to search.

arch.notes:
[Follow the document path into the index, then trace each incoming query path.] Start with a passage. Stella runs 24 layers at width 1,024, averages the token states, applies its square dense projection, and normalizes the result. I store the vector in fp16. Tonight's passages are already at the center of the diagram. HNSW links those document vectors, and binary quantization gives me a compact version for the candidate search. A 1,024-dimensional vector takes 128 bytes at one bit per dimension. Across 2.7 million passages that's 343 MB of codes in RAM. The fp16 originals take 5.49 GB on disk for rescoring. Those figures cover the vector data. The graph and sparse index have their own storage.

Now follow a query. Stella adds its instruction prompt and uses its usual encoder. Nano starts from bge-small. I mean-pool layers 12, eight, and four in that order, join the 1,152 features, and project into Stella's 1,024 dimensions. Zero tokenizes, gathers dequantized rows, weights them by the square root of their counts, and normalizes the sum.

The compatibility test is whether those outputs rank the stored passages well. I can try each encoder against the very same vectors and graph, even on successive requests. I call that family Constella.

footprint.notes:
[Point to the file and peak RSS columns.] If you're trying to fit this on a device, read those as two different bills. Stella has about 435 million parameters in a 1,670 MiB export. It peaks at 2,812 MiB of RAM and takes about two seconds to load with a warm file cache. Nano has 34.5 million parameters and peaks at 317 MiB. On my M5 Pro, the median encode drops from 31.6 to 2.25 milliseconds.

Zero is where file size can trip you up. Its 31 MB int8 table holds 31.3 million values. The shipped files also have an fp16 reference table, and the serving loader expands the int8 rows to 125 MB in fp32. The process peaks at 360 MiB, even though the median encode is 44 microseconds.

Those are encoder measurements. I can run the big document encoder in the cloud and run the query encoder where the user is.

cloud.notes:
If the laptop made Stella look easy to serve, try putting a price on the query rate. I rented a GCP c4-standard-8 with eight vCPUs at about 40 cents an hour. I ran eight workers on batches of one. They kept sending queries as fast as they finished them.

[Point to the throughput and VM columns.] At saturation I measured about 18 Stella queries a second. That projects to about $6 per million at peak and 56 VMs to encode 1,000 queries a second. Nano did 464 a second, so 24 cents per million at peak and three VMs for the same rate. Zero did about 67,000 a second. The price at that measured peak is $0.0016 per million, about a sixth of a cent.

A dedicated Zero VM serving 1,000 queries a second would use only about 1.5% of that measured capacity. You'd still pay for the VM, so the bill works out to about 11 cents per million. All of that is for making the vectors. The search meter starts where this one stops.

distill.notes:
A vector of the right length is easy to make. I need one whose dot products make sense against Stella's passages. I already have a function that makes those vectors. That's the teacher. I run it once over the training texts and save its normalized outputs. Then I fit a student to land near those outputs. I can score the resulting queries directly against the document vectors I already have.

For Nano I use Stella's query output for a query and its document output for a passage. Those vectors are the supervision, so Nano can train without relevance judgments. Zero also uses queries paired with relevant passages, in both training phases. With a new teacher, our historical estimate for preparing Zero's targets was eight to 12 hours of encoding.

The smallest student I tried has a single row of numbers per token. Here's where the work goes when I type a query.

zero-mech.notes:
[Follow the highlighted rows from the tokens to the output.] Take "cheap flights Paris to Rome." Stella's WordPiece tokenizer gives me IDs. Each ID is an address in a 30,522-row table. Each row has 1,024 values, the same width as the document vectors. If I repeat a token, its contribution grows with the square root of the count. The repeat matters a little less each time. I pool a weighted mean and normalize it. If you work with Lucene, think of looking up term weights, except what comes out here is one dense query vector.

The stored rows are int8 with one scale per row. The formula shows the scale because the raw integer rows need it to represent the right values. The released NumPy encoder applies those scales at load and keeps fp32 rows in memory. Per query it gathers those rows and pools them.

I started the table from Stella's encodings of individual tokens. The desktop RTX 3080 fit the pooled queries to Stella's vectors and matched its scores on paired examples. A second pass trained the table to rank relevant documents ahead of negatives using the frozen document vectors.

Follow what survives that pooling step. I get the row and how often it appears. What happens if I keep the words and change the route?

order.notes:
I can keep every word and still ask for a different ticket. Read "Paris to Rome," then "Rome to Paris." Zero gets the same bag of tokens. The same rows get the same weights, so I get exactly the same vector. Whatever the search does for the first route, it does for the second route too.

I wanted to see what the contextual encoders could do with the order. I wrote 24 pairs where reversing the direction changes the answer. Each pair got two passages, one for each direction. To pass, an encoder had to put the intended passage first on both queries. Stella changed its query vector on every reversal. That's an easy test for context to pass. Now watch the ranking test.

[click] Stella got both directions right on four of 24 pairs. All four were unit conversions. Nano got two pairs right, and Zero got zero. It's a small exploratory probe. The query and passage pairs are in the repository if you want to try them with another encoder. The exercise gave me two things to check separately. Can the encoder tell the queries apart? Do the changed vectors put the right passage first?

zero-train.notes:
[Point to Align and Rank. Leave the source list for questions.] I started with Stella's encoding of each token and gave its scalar weight the token's inverse document frequency. Alignment runs for 16,000 batches of 512. Half the batch gets cosine loss alone. The paired half also matches Stella's softmax over one positive and 31 distractors using KL divergence at temperature 0.02.

Then I ran 2,500 ranking steps against a bank of frozen vectors, with 32,768 bank negatives per step. I masked known positives and any negative Stella scored above the positive minus 0.02. That keeps plausible answers out of the penalty. I folded the weights into the int8 rows and kept one scale per row. With targets ready, the estimate was about 20 minutes on a 10 GB 3080.

[If asked about the data, name Amazon ESCI, FEVER, HotpotQA, SQuAD, Mr. TyDi, NQ Open, and TriviaQA. All training sources permit commercial derived weights.]

nano.notes:
Order is a reason I'd still want a transformer on the query side. I used the small bge backbone for Nano. The last layer has 384 channels. A linear head fed just that layer can only move within a slice of Stella's space with at most 384 dimensions. Pool layers 12, eight, and four, and the head gets 1,152 features to work with. It still outputs a 1,024-dimensional vector for the existing index.

I initialize the head with a ridge fit. Then I train the backbone and head together on squared error between normalized vectors. I alternate three query batches and one passage batch, each with its corresponding Stella target. The query pool had about 3.5 million texts. Qwen3-8B generated 834,000 of them in seven forms. Training sampled evenly across 12 forms from the combined pool.

The recipe search ran on the desktop 3080. The final training run took 57.3 A100 hours, about $95. I pay for that fit once. To see if it was worth paying for, I need to look at the rankings.

bench.notes:
[Trace the Stella, Nano, and Zero rows where the document index stays the same.] I scored every document exactly here. That lets me ask what the query representation does to ranking before I make the graph approximate anything. The table is a mean of nDCG@10 across 15 BEIR datasets. Nano kept 90.5% of Stella's score and Zero kept 81.4%. One way I'd spend some of Zero's savings is a lexical branch. I combine Zero and BM25 over the same passages with distribution-based score fusion. Retention comes back to 87.9%. The 44 microseconds measures dense encoding alone. Budget for sparse encoding, a second search, and fusion.

The comparison rows answer a different question. Nano scored 0.508 on Stella's index. On their own indexes, bge-small scored 0.517 and LEAF scored 0.540. Those runs change the document representation as well as the query encoder. If I want three query budgets from one ingestion pipeline, the first three rows are the ones I can run together.

And the average is a poor stand-in for your traffic. In these results, Zero kept about two thirds of Stella on TREC-COVID and FiQA, and 95% on Quora. We've timed encoders and we've measured exact ranking. Now I want to put the two together on the same workload.

bet.notes:
For the Natural Questions workload on this laptop, Zero's median encode was 0.032 milliseconds. Nano's was 1.63. That makes Zero about 51 times faster at the point where I have a vector in hand.

[click] Keep the clock running until the search results come back. What would you bet on for the median request speedup? Shout a number or put it in the Zoom chat.

[Take guesses. Keep a guess to compare with the replay.] I'll keep that guess for when we get back to the request medians. First, watch where the two lanes spend their time.

race.notes:
[Switch the shared screen to the demo. Open Race and press Space. Play the recorded fallback if the replay is unavailable.]

I measured the same 3,452 questions one encoder at a time on this laptop. The lanes replay those timings side by side. They can line up on screen because I gave each encoder its own run. The dense lanes search one Stella index with 2.7 million Wikipedia passages. Qdrant Edge runs in the same process as the demo.

Watch the seam where teal turns orange. Teal ends when there's a query vector. Orange runs from there until the graph search and rescoring are done. Start with Stella. See how long the transformer keeps the search waiting. Then follow Zero on the same question. That little flash of teal is why I wanted to put a clock on the whole thing.

[Let the replay run. Point out the encoding and search segments for Nano and Zero on the same query. Compare the full timings shown for the two lanes.] [Give Zoom time to follow the highlighted segments.]

[Read back the displayed Nano and Zero totals and the speedup for the full request.] Across the whole replay, Nano spent 7.24 seconds encoding and searching. Zero spent 3.14. That's 2.30 times faster on the sum of all the requests. Search took 87% of Zero's time on that clock.

[Bring back a guess from the room or Zoom.] A slow request adds its full time to that finish clock. Our bet was about the median request, so I need a different number from this same exploratory run. I also need to show what each lane gave back for the time we spent.

[Return to the split slide.]

split.notes:
[Point to the p50 total column.] Here's the answer to the bet. Nano's median request took 2.04 milliseconds. Zero's took 0.86. That's 2.4 times faster. I added encode and search for each query first, then took the median. The bars use the two component medians to show where the time goes. On those bars, search is 96% of Zero's time. The replay clock gave us 2.3 times across all 3,452 requests.

[Move across to the relevance column.] Put the scores beside those times. Zero scored 0.510 and Nano scored 0.579. For Nano and Stella, I picked the fastest median within 1% of that encoder's own exact nDCG@10. Nano gets there at ef 512 and fourfold oversampling, against an exact score of 0.584. Stella gets 0.631 against 0.637 at ef 256 and fourfold oversampling. Zero's best tested point is ef 1,024 with eightfold oversampling. That still falls about 1.5% short of its exact 0.517, so it misses the 99% target. The exact scores match the registered paper rows. BM25 gives another reference on this shard. It took 1.12 milliseconds at 0.301.

[If asked about training overlap, both students trained on questions from NQ Open. This sweep uses the NQ test queries.]

Binary quantization makes the candidate pass cheap enough to explore wider. Hamming distance compares 128-byte sign codes in RAM. Then we rescore the top oversampling times k candidates with the original fp16 vectors. So why did Zero need to go so wide in the first place?

recovery.notes:
HNSW links document vectors to other document vectors. I leave all those links in place when I change the query encoder. The new vector changes which documents the search scores highly as it walks. To see what that walk costs me, I get an exact top ten for each encoder and check how many of its own neighbors the graph finds.

[Start at Stella at ef 32. Follow across to Zero at ef 1,024.] Hold oversampling at four for this plot. On NQ, Zero searched at the farthest setting we tested and still recovered less of its own exact top ten than Stella did at the first setting. In the paper's 25-model study, I started from each teacher's recovery at ef 64. The median lookup table needed ef 256 for the same recovery on FiQA and TREC-COVID. On SCIDOCS it needed 128.

I got a clue before even fitting a table. Take the teacher's queries and divide their nearest-document distance by the typical distance between neighboring documents. When the queries sat farther from the documents by that measure, tables tended to lose more recovery. The rank correlation with the signed gap was minus 0.64.

That's a count of neighbors. If the question is how much judged relevance I lose, use nDCG. On TREC-COVID, only 12 of 25 models needed a wider search to match their teacher's nDCG loss. Let's try turning the search breadth on a query one of you cares about.

live.notes:
[Switch to the demo and open Live. Take a query from the room or Zoom chat. Enter it and run all four columns.]

Give me something you'd look up in Wikipedia. I'll send that same text through all three dense encoders against the same document vectors. BM25 searches the same passages as a lexical reference. Watch the boundary between encode and search, then read the title and first line of each top passage with me. Which would you open? What were you hoping to find?

[Read the first results aloud. Ask what the audience wanted to find. Switch on the exact check and compare the dense columns.]

In the Zero column, that count asks how many of Zero's exact top ten the graph found. Stella's column uses Stella's list. Both can show ten even if they send you to different pages. Keep your answer about which page you'd open in mind while I change the search.

[Lower hnsw_ef and rerun. Raise it and rerun. Read out the search times and exact-neighbor counts that appear. If the first query barely changes, take another from the room or Zoom. Use the recorded fallback if live search is unavailable.]

I kept the text, the encoders, and the index fixed. Watch whether the extra search time brought any exact neighbors back. [If the count stays put, compare the search times at equal recovery.] And check whether the page you'd open changed. That last question is what I'd ask across a batch of judged queries from my traffic. The same batch can save time if I'm still deciding which document encoder to build around.

[Return to the deck.]

worst.notes:
If you're still choosing a document encoder, here's a pitfall I hit. I expected the strongest retriever to give me the strongest cheap student. I fit lookup tables for 10 public embedding models in the registered comparison. Each kept its own document index. The ridge fit takes token counts divided by query length as X. It uses teacher query vectors as Y and pulls the fitted rows toward the teacher's encodings of individual tokens.

[Point to gte-large, then Stella.] Right is better original ranking. Up is better table ranking. Over six BEIR datasets with exact search, gte-large-en-v1.5 went from 0.5970 to 0.2455, the best original and the weakest table. Stella went from 0.5745 to 0.3974 and gave me the best table of the ten. Close vector agreement could still go with worse ranking. A screening fit took four to seven minutes on an A100. For that price, I can put it on my judged queries.

recipe.notes:
You need 0.55 nDCG@10 and a 3 millisecond p95. Which encoder ships?

[Give the room and Zoom a moment. Point to the 0.55 row.] Nano at ef 64 with fourfold oversampling. It scored 0.554 with a 2.12 millisecond p95 and a 1.74 millisecond median. At a floor of 0.50, Zero at ef 512 and fourfold oversampling gets the job at 0.49 milliseconds median and 0.96 p95. Raise the floor to 0.62 with the same budget and every tested configuration falls outside the constraints. Only Stella clears that relevance floor. It needs about 34.6 milliseconds at p95, so a 35 millisecond budget would let it in.

I'd run this on my own traffic. Sample queries and judge the results. Set the relevance floor and the p95 budget before looking at the sweep. Run each encoder with exact search against the existing index to establish its ranking quality. Then sweep search breadth and oversampling for each encoder and time encoding plus search on each request. From the configurations that clear both constraints, ship the one with the lowest median.

If you have several budgets, carry ef and oversampling with each encoder choice. The measurements here come from one exploratory laptop run. The decision you'll make comes from your queries and the time your users can wait.

close.notes:
If you've already paid for an index, put it to work on the next encoder experiment. Start with a batch of queries you can judge. That will tell you how far you can turn the query encoder dial on the index you have.

[Leave the paper preview and repository QR on screen when available.] [QR: paper preview and repository] Zero, Nano, and the Stella document encoder are on Hugging Face and in FastEmbed. The install command is on screen. The QR links the models and the code, and the paper preview has the measurements and how I made them. Thanks for the queries, in the room and on Zoom.

b-datasets.notes: Quora was at 95% of Stella's score for Zero, while TREC-COVID and FiQA were both at 67%. Nano kept 85% to 99% except on FEVER. Zero's training pool included FEVER, and Nano's excluded it.

b-msmarco.notes: On the binary-quantized million-passage MS MARCO index, I picked the fastest tested setting within 1% of each encoder's own exact score. Summing the separate encode and search medians put Zero at about 19 times Stella's speed and 2.2 times Nano's, at lower nDCG@10. In the whole-request comparison on those passages, BM25 saved 0.45 milliseconds at 0.66 versus 1.11, and Zero scored 24.5% higher at 0.6094 versus 0.4895.

b-edge.notes: I put all 30,522 rows in a Qdrant Edge shard and fetched them by token ID before pooling and searching. Across 500 queries, the maximum difference from the released encoder was zero. The lookup added about a quarter millisecond on this laptop compared with the in-memory NumPy table.

b-routing.notes: With relevance judgments to pick Zero or Nano, the oracle scored 0.547 against 0.516 for always running Nano. At the same Nano share, query length, subwords per word, and pooled vector norm beat random routing by at most 0.005 nDCG@10. I'd start by using the encoder budget that fits what the user is doing, such as typing, pausing, or submitting.

b-teachers.notes: Across 26 models, the rank correlation between teacher and table nDCG was 0.09, with a 95% interval from minus 0.39 to plus 0.52. Together, teacher ranking and dimensionality predicted table quality, with standardized coefficients of plus 0.63 and minus 0.64 in the exploratory fit. Two e5 tables reached 0.90 and 0.89 mean cosine to their teachers against Stella's 0.78, yet ranked worse, so I'd decide by measuring ranking.

b-predictor.notes: Before fitting the table I can compare a teacher query's nearest-document distance with the typical nearest-neighbor distance between documents. Across 75 model and workload pairs, that ratio had a rank correlation of minus 0.64 with the signed recovery gap, and predictions on held-out model families correlated at plus 0.64. The gap also appeared with LightRetriever on FiQA, where its lookup path recovered 3.6 percentage points fewer of its own exact neighbors and needed four times the search breadth to match recovery.
